article.overview: A low-frequency radio antenna is a receiver that detects radio emission at the long-wavelength end of the radio spectrum. The name describes a class of instruments rather than one standard design. The examples reviewed for this article are lunar surface antennas that record radio emission between a few kilohertz and about 50 MHz. Earth's ionosphere blocks observations below about 15 MHz from the ground, so these measurements must be made from the Moon [3][4].
article.description: Low-frequency radio antennas on the lunar surface are long metallic elements that are stowed for launch and deployed after landing. The reviewed examples use elements of roughly 2.5 m to 6 m in length. Each antenna produces a small voltage that is amplified, digitised and passed to a receiver or spectrometer. The spectrometer computes power spectra and, in some designs, cross-correlations between antennas that give the polarisation (Stokes) parameters of the radio sky [2][4][5]. The instruments are not interchangeable: they differ in frequency coverage, antenna geometry, receiver design and mission status, and each is described separately below.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
The main purpose of lunar low-frequency antennas is to observe the radio sky in a band that is hard to reach from Earth. The LuSEE-Night design aims to measure the galactic synchrotron spectrum below 50 MHz, the local magnetic field, exo-ionospheric density and occultations as the Sun and planets set below the horizon. It is also intended as a pathfinder for measurements of the 21 cm 'Dark Ages' signal [1][2][3]. The ROLSES instrument is designed to measure the photoelectron sheath density, which relates to surface charging, and to record radio interference from human activity [3][4].

The Chang'e-4 Low-Frequency Radio Spectrometer, operating on the lunar farside, was used in a 2026 analysis searching for periodic artificial signals. The authors report no credible periodic candidate in the sample they analysed [5].

The FARSIDE concept is a proposed 10 km interferometric array of 128 dipole-antenna pairs. Its stated goals include imaging coronal mass ejections beyond two solar radii and monitoring auroral radio emission from Uranus and Neptune. FARSIDE and its PRIME precursor are proposals and have not been flown [3].
article.operating_principle: A radio antenna responds to the electric field of incoming waves. The resulting voltage is amplified by a low-noise front end, digitised at a high sampling rate and processed. In the LuSEE-Night design, each of four monopole channels is read as a single-ended voltage through a high-impedance, low-noise JFET front end. The signals are sampled at 102.4 million samples per second, and an FPGA computes auto- and cross-correlation spectra. Stokes parameters can be derived from the cross-correlations alone, which avoids antenna shot noise [2]. The ROLSES instrument digitises each channel to 14 bits at 120 million samples per second and performs an onboard FFT. It stores time-averaged spectra and also telemetres raw waveforms, which are useful for studying dust impacts [4].
article.scientific_importance: Low-frequency radio measurements from the Moon address questions that are difficult to study from Earth. Earth's ionosphere prevents ground-based observation below about 15 MHz [4], and terrestrial radio noise limits sensitive measurements. The lunar farside is shielded from Earth's radio emission and from the lander's own interference, which makes it attractive for these observations [1][5]. The reviewed instruments are also pathfinders that test techniques for larger arrays such as the proposed FARSIDE array [3].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a lunar low-frequency radio antenna. The examples below describe specific flown instruments, a pre-launch design and a proposed concept. They are not directly comparable, and no value is given where the reviewed sources are silent.

examples.name: Chang'e-4 Low-Frequency Radio Spectrometer (LFRS)
examples.type: Flown lunar farside lander radio spectrometer
examples.status: Flown; observations began 5 January 2019 and continued for several years (no end date given)
examples.antenna_configuration: Three orthogonal 5 m dipoles (A, B, C) and one 20 cm short antenna (D) parallel to the lander wall; short antenna used for background-noise mitigation and dipole calibration
examples.mounting: Top of the Chang'e-4 lander, fixed antenna orientations
examples.frequency_resolution: At most 10 kHz (low band); at most 200 kHz (high band). The paper's sensitivity estimate uses about 19 kHz, which is not reconciled with the 10 kHz figure.

examples.name: ROLSES on Intuitive Machines IM-1 (Odysseus)
examples.type: Flown lunar surface radio monopole instrument
examples.status: Flown; initial observations during transit and surface operations reported; operating duration not stated
examples.antenna_configuration: Four 2.5 m radio monopole antennas, stowed for launch and deployed after landing with a frangibolt mechanism
examples.digitisation: 14 bits at 120 million samples per second per channel; onboard FPGA FFT; time-averaged spectra stored and raw waveforms telemetred
examples.landing_site_as_reported: Close to the south pole at Malapert A (80 S); the paper also mentions a tilted landing

examples.name: LuSEE-Night
examples.type: Pre-launch lunar farside radio experiment (design as described in 2023)
examples.status: In development as of the January 2023 paper; launch and landing targeted for late 2025 to early 2026 in that paper; launch not confirmed in reviewed sources
examples.antenna_configuration: Two orthogonal, co-linear dipole pairs, about 6 m tip to tip, built from 3 m BeCu stacer elements; stacers self-deploy into a rigid tube of about 1 cm diameter; motor-driven carousel rotates antennas in the plane of the lunar surface during the lunar day
examples.frequency_range: Full-Stokes spectral measurements up to 50 MHz (calibration discussion extends the band to 51.2 MHz)
examples.receiver: 4-channel, 50 MHz Nyquist baseband receiver; high-impedance JFET front end per monopole; sampling at 102.4 million samples per second; FPGA auto- and cross-correlation spectra; based on the Radio Frequency Spectrometer flown on Parker Solar Probe FIELDS
examples.power: Solar cells; battery of about 40 kg for the lunar night; system described as power-positive after sunrise

examples.name: FARSIDE (proposed) and PRIME precursor
examples.type: Proposed interferometric array concept and risk-reduction precursor
examples.antenna_configuration: FARSIDE: 128 pairs of dipole antennas in a 10 km interferometric array. PRIME: six-antenna-node array (antenna type not stated).

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions are instrument-specific: Chang'e-4 dipoles 5 m; ROLSES monopoles 2.5 m; LuSEE-Night dipoles about 6 m tip to tip; FARSIDE array 10 km in diameter. Enclosure or housing dimensions are not stated in the reviewed sources for these instruments.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Total instrument mass is not stated in the reviewed sources for any example. The only mass figure is the LuSEE-Night battery of about 40 kg [2]; it is a subsystem mass, not the payload mass.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: LuSEE-Night uses solar cells and a battery of about 40 kg to power the system through the lunar night, and is described as power-positive after sunrise [2]. Power figures for the Chang'e-4 LFRS and ROLSES are not stated in the reviewed text [4][5].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
The lunar night lasts about 14 Earth days, so a surface radio antenna that operates through it must survive long periods without solar power. The LuSEE-Night design thermally isolates its electronics and relies on night-time operating power to keep them warm. It rejects daytime heat through south-facing parabolic reflector radiators [2]. These radiators need a view of dark sky, so the paper states that the landing site must lie north or south of the lunar equator [2]. The paper also states that the lander must stop operating before the first nightfall and remain powered off for the mission [2].

The farside location is chosen to avoid lander electromagnetic interference and Earth's radio noise [1]. The ROLSES science goals include measuring radio interference from human activity [3].
article.limitations: Lunar surface antennas are sensitive to their local environment, including interference from the lander and from human activity on the surface [1][3]. Ground-based observation below about 15 MHz is not possible [4], so these instruments depend on a surface mission and can only record data during that mission's operating life. The examples differ in frequency coverage, antenna length and receiver design, and their values should not be combined as if they came from one instrument [2][4][5]. Mass and power figures are unpublished for several examples in the reviewed sources.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: These examples are surface instruments delivered by a lander and deployed after landing. The reviewed sources do not describe Earth integration, launch or lunar transfer in detail. LuSEE-Night is intended for a NASA CLPS delivery, designated CS-3 in the 2023 paper; ROLSES flew on the Intuitive Machines IM-1 lander; the Chang'e-4 LFRS flew on the Chang'e-4 lander.
transportation_process: Mount the antennas and receiver on the lander: Chang'e-4 LFRS dipoles were fixed to the top of the lander [5].
Launch and transfer to the Moon: not described in detail in the reviewed sources.
Land on the lunar surface with the lander: ROLSES on IM-1 [4]; LuSEE-Night planned for a CLPS lander [1][2].
Deploy the antennas: LuSEE-Night stacers self-deploy from stored spring energy [2]; ROLSES monopoles are released by a frangibolt mechanism [4].
Connect power and communications: LuSEE-Night is planned to use ESA's Lunar Pathfinder relay for S-band communications [2].
Operate through the lunar day and stop before the first lunar night: stated as a requirement for LuSEE-Night, which must remain powered off thereafter [2].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Stored-energy self-deployment of stacer elements (LuSEE-Night) [2]; frangibolt release of stowed monopoles (ROLSES) [4]; fixed lander-mounted dipoles (Chang'e-4 LFRS) [5]. The LuSEE-Night antenna carousel is motor-driven and operates only during the lunar day [2].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: ROLSES flew on IM-1 [4]. The Chang'e-4 LFRS flew on the Chang'e-4 lander, the first mission to soft-land on the lunar farside [5]. LuSEE-Night had not been confirmed as flown in the reviewed sources [1][2].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No verified interface data for any named lander were found in the reviewed sources, so no compatibility is asserted. Mission facts for IM-1 and Chang'e-4 are listed above; they are not compatibility assessments. A future compatibility assessment would need the lander's mass, dimensions, mounting interface, landing loads, power and communications architecture.

article.historical_significance:
Chang'e-4 was the first mission to soft-land on the lunar farside. Its Low-Frequency Radio Spectrometer began observations on 5 January 2019 [5]. A 2026 analysis of its data searched for periodic artificial signals and found no credible candidate [5].

A 2021 roadmap paper describes ROLSES and LuSEE as the first in a sequence of CLPS-delivered radio pathfinders for the proposed FARSIDE array [3]. ROLSES flew on IM-1 [4]. LuSEE-Night has not been confirmed as flown [1][2].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The payload name describes a class of instruments rather than one standard design. The examples reviewed are not interchangeable, and every value above must be read together with its instrument and source. The main evidence gaps are the LuSEE-Night launch status, the conflicting ROLSES landing descriptions, the unresolved PRIME status, the unreconciled Chang'e-4 sensitivity figures, and missing mass, power and temperature data. A secondary search summary associating LuSEE-Night with Firefly's Blue Ghost Mission 2 and a secondary summary of ROLSES landing and operation were not verified against primary sources and are not relied on as facts.

image_handling.url_policy: All source URLs in this file have query strings and fragments removed. No image asset URLs were verified, so no image objects are included; all image arrays are empty by design.

data_quality_notes: No image asset URLs were verified from official pages, so the image registry and all section-level image arrays are empty. image_urls_added is false.
Chang'e-4 LFRS: the paper gives 10 kHz low-band resolution and also uses about 19 kHz in its sensitivity estimate. Both values are reported; they are not reconciled.

ROLSES on IM-1: the paper summary describes a tilted landing. A secondary search summary described a hard landing with brief post-landing operation and gave launch and landing dates of 15 and 22 February 2024. These are unverified and conflict; they are not used as facts.

LuSEE-Night: the detailed description is from a January 2023 pre-launch paper. Its launch and landing dates in that paper were late 2025 to early 2026. A secondary 2026 summary associates it with Firefly's Blue Ghost Mission 2, which had not launched in the sources found. Launch status is unconfirmed.

PRIME radio array: no current status was found. A 2026 NASA slide set uses the name PRIME-1 for a different experiment (the Polar Resources Ice Mining Experiment on IM-2), so search results for that name are not evidence about the radio array.

Mass, power and operating-temperature figures are unpublished in the reviewed sources for most examples. The only mass figure is the approximately 40 kg LuSEE-Night battery, which is a subsystem mass and not a payload mass.

Primary full-text PDFs of the arXiv papers could not be read by the fetch tool; details were taken from arXiv abstract pages, the ar5iv HTML rendering of arXiv:2301.10345, and the arXiv HTML version of arXiv:2604.07920v2. Full-text verification of 2102.02331 and 2603.22600 remains open.
